Gillespie et al. conducted a study in 2014 published in the New England Journal of Medicine that evaluated four-month treatment regimens for drug-sensitive tuberculosis using moxifloxacin. The study demonstrated the potential of moxifloxacin-based regimens in shortening treatment duration while maintaining efficacy. 2. Jawahar et al. performed a randomized clinical trial in 2013, published in PLOS One, comparing thrice-weekly four-month regimens containing either moxifloxacin or gatifloxacin for the treatment of newly diagnosed sputum-positive pulmonary tuberculosis. The findings provided insights into the effectiveness of these fluoroquinolone-based regimens. 3. The World Health Organization (WHO) released the Global Tuberculosis Report 2014, which provided a comprehensive overview of the global burden of tuberculosis, including epidemiological data, treatment outcomes, and challenges in TB control. 4. Vierenfeldt et al. published a longitudinal cohort study in BMJ Open in 2014, which highlighted the impact of treatment delays on the clinical severity of tuberculosis. The study emphasized the importance of timely diagnosis and treatment initiation to improve patient outcomes. 5. Harris et al. conducted a systematic review in 2016, published in BMC Infectious Diseases, examining the effects of early versus late treatment initiation on outcomes in patients with multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB). The review underscored the benefits of prompt treatment initiation in improving survival and reducing adverse outcomes. 6. The International Standards for Tuberculosis Care (3rd edition) was published by TB CARE 1, providing evidence-based guidelines for the diagnosis, treatment, and management of tuberculosis, with a focus on improving patient care and outcomes. 7. Harris et al. also conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis in 2016, published in BMC Infectious Diseases, to evaluate the role of surgery in the treatment of MDR-TB. The findings suggested that surgery could be a valuable adjunct to medical therapy in select cases, particularly for patients with localized disease. 8. The Priorities for Tuberculosis Research report, developed by the Disease Reference Group on TB, Leprosy, and Buruli Ulcer, outlined key research areas to address gaps in TB prevention, diagnosis, and treatment. 9. Mitnick et al. published an updated research agenda in 2016 in PLOS One for the programmatic management of drug-resistant tuberculosis. The agenda highlighted the need for further studies on new drugs, shorter regimens, and innovative treatment strategies. 10. The WHO released guidelines on the management of latent tuberculosis infection, emphasizing the importance of identifying and treating individuals at high risk of progression to active TB to reduce transmission and disease burden. 11. The WHO convened a meeting in November 2015 to finalize recommendations for the treatment of drug-resistant tuberculosis. Discussions included the evaluation of regimens for isoniazid-resistant TB, levels of resistance to pyrazinamide and fluoroquinolones, and research priorities for MDR-TB treatment. 12. The WHO 2016 treatment guidelines for drug-resistant tuberculosis provided updated recommendations based on evidence from clinical trials and systematic reviews. These guidelines addressed the use of new drugs, shorter regimens, and individualized treatment approaches for MDR-TB and extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB). 13. The guidelines also included PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcomes) questions to evaluate the effectiveness of individual drugs and regimens for MDR-TB and XDR-TB. These questions focused on outcomes such as cure rates, culture conversion, relapse, survival, adverse reactions, and the acquisition of additional drug resistance. 14. The guidelines emphasized the importance of using at least four effective second-line drugs plus pyrazinamide in MDR-TB regimens, with a total treatment duration of at least 18 months after culture conversion. Shorter regimens lasting 9–12 months were also evaluated for their potential to improve adherence and reduce treatment burden. 15. The role of elective surgery in MDR-TB treatment was discussed, with evidence suggesting that surgery may be beneficial in select cases, particularly for patients with localized disease or extensive drug resistance. 16. The guidelines highlighted the need for further research on the use of newer drugs such as bedaquiline and delamanid, as definitive recommendations would depend on the results of ongoing Phase III clinical trials. 17. The WHO also addressed the importance of timely treatment initiation, recommending that treatment for MDR-TB should begin within four weeks of diagnosis to improve outcomes and reduce the risk of disease progression. 18. 19. The WHO guideline development process involved contributions from a diverse group of experts, including clinicians, researchers, and public health professionals, who reviewed evidence and provided recommendations to improve TB care globally. 20. The guidelines also emphasized the importance of adherence to treatment and strategies to minimize interruptions, as non-adherence could lead to treatment failure, relapse, and the development of additional drug resistance.
